source.text: Kumārajīva, trans., Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (Taishō T235); the 32 sections follow Prince Zhaoming of Liang
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

k01.heading: 1. The Occasion of the Assembly
k01.plain: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at Jeta Grove in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty monks. At mealtime the World-Honored One put on his robe, took up his bowl and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having begged from house to house in turn, he returned to where he had been staying and ate. Then he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat and sat down.
k01.commentary: How the assembly came about. With no great miracle, the sutra begins in the everyday: begging for food, eating, washing the feet, sitting down. This ordinary life itself is seen as the model of a life that dwells nowhere.

k02.heading: 2. Subhūti Makes His Request
k02.plain: Then the elder Subhūti rose from his seat in the assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms respectfully and said to the Buddha: "How rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cares well for the bodhisattvas and instructs them well. World-Honored One, when good men and good women set their minds on supreme, perfect awakening, how should they abide, and how should they subdue their minds?" The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti. It is as you say. Now listen closely and I will tell you. Those who set their minds on supreme awakening should abide thus and subdue their minds thus." "Yes, World-Honored One. I gladly wish to hear."
k02.commentary: "How should one abide, and how should one subdue the mind?" is the question that drives the whole Diamond Sutra. Subhūti, who understood emptiness best of all the disciples, is called "foremost in understanding emptiness."

k03.heading: 3. The True Teaching of the Great Vehicle
k03.plain: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds like this: 'All kinds of beings, whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture or by transformation, with form or without form, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception, I will lead them all into nirvana without remainder and liberate them.' Yet though measureless, countless, boundless beings are liberated in this way, in truth no being is liberated. Why? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva holds the notion of a self, a person, a being or a life, they are not a bodhisattva."
k03.commentary: The true meaning of the Great Vehicle. A bodhisattva needs both the great vow to save all beings and the wisdom not to be caught by an "I" who saves or "beings" who are saved.

k04.heading: 4. Wondrous Practice Without Abiding
k04.plain: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give without abiding in anything: giving without abiding in form, giving without abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch or objects of mind. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give like this, not abiding in appearances. Why? If a bodhisattva gives without abiding in appearances, the merit is beyond measure. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space to the east be measured?" "No, World-Honored One." "Can the space to the south, west and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below be measured?" "No, World-Honored One." "The merit of a bodhisattva who gives without abiding in appearances is likewise beyond measure. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should abide only as I have taught."
k04.commentary: Giving without abiding in appearances: generosity not caught by the thought of giving, the receiver or the gift. Like space, it has no bounds, so its merit is endless.

k05.heading: 5. Seeing the Truth as It Is
k05.plain: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by his bodily form?" "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by bodily form. Why? The bodily form the Tathāgata speaks of is not bodily form." The Buddha said to Subhūti: "All that has form is illusory. If you see all forms as no-form, you see the Tathāgata."
k05.commentary: "All that has form is illusory; if you see all forms as no-form, you see the Tathāgata" is the first four-line verse of the Diamond Sutra and the most widely recited.

k06.heading: 6. Rare Is True Faith
k06.plain: Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, will there be beings who hear these words and give rise to true faith?" "Do not say so. Even five hundred years after the Tathāgata's passing, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit who have faith in these words and take them as true. Know that such people have planted roots of goodness not just with one, two, three, four or five Buddhas, but with countless thousands of millions of Buddhas. If on hearing these words they give rise to pure faith even for a single thought, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that they gain measureless merit. Why? These beings have no notion of self, person, being or life; no notion of dharma, and no notion of non-dharma. If the mind grasps at appearances, it clings to self, person, being and life; so too if it grasps at the notion of dharma, or at the notion of non-dharma. Therefore do not grasp at dharma, and do not grasp at non-dharma. That is why the Tathāgata always says: Monks, know that my teaching is like a raft. Even the Dharma must be let go, how much more what is not the Dharma."
k06.commentary: The parable of the raft. Once you have crossed the river you do not carry the raft on your back; likewise the teaching is a means of reaching awakening, not something to hold on to.

k07.heading: 7. Nothing Attained, Nothing Taught
k07.plain: "Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained supreme, perfect awakening? Is there a Dharma the Tathāgata has taught?" Subhūti answered: "As I understand the meaning of the Buddha's words, there is no fixed dharma called supreme, perfect awakening, and no fixed dharma the Tathāgata can teach. Why? The Dharma the Tathāgata teaches cannot be grasped or spoken; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma. All the sages differ only through the unconditioned."
k07.commentary: Awakening is not something "attained" like a possession, and the Dharma is not a fixed doctrine. The sages differ only in how deeply they have realized the unconditioned.

k08.heading: 8. Born of the Dharma
k08.plain: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone filled the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would their merit be great?" "Very great, World-Honored One. That merit is not the nature of merit; that is why the Tathāgata says the merit is great." "If someone else receives and keeps even a single four-line verse of this sutra and explains it to others, their merit surpasses that. Why? All Buddhas and the Dharma of the Buddhas' supreme awakening come from this sutra. Subhūti, what is called the Buddha-Dharma is not the Buddha-Dharma."
k08.commentary: The gift of Dharma is greater than material gifts. "The Buddha-Dharma is not the Buddha-Dharma" is the Diamond Sutra's characteristic logic, telling us not to cling even to the name "Buddha-Dharma."

k09.heading: 9. The One Mark Is No Mark
k09.plain: "Subhūti, does a stream-enterer think, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?" "No. A stream-enterer is called 'one who has entered the stream,' but there is nowhere entered. Not entering form, sound, smell, taste, touch or objects of mind is what is called a stream-enterer." The once-returner ("one who comes and goes once more") and the non-returner ("one who does not come back") are likewise so called because in truth there is no coming or going. "Does an arhat think, 'I have attained the way of the arhat'?" "No. In truth there is no dharma called arhat. To think so would be clinging to self, person, being and life. The Buddha has said that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention, that I am foremost among people, the first arhat free of desire; yet I do not think, 'I am an arhat free of desire.' If I thought so, the World-Honored One would not call Subhūti 'one who delights in the peaceful practice.' Because Subhūti in truth does nothing, he is called one who delights in the peaceful practice."
k09.commentary: Even the four stages of the śrāvaka's awakening are true awakening only when there is no thought of having "attained" them. Subhūti himself is given as the example.

k10.heading: 10. Adorning the Pure Land
k10.plain: "Subhūti, when the Tathāgata was long ago with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he attain any dharma?" "No. When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly attained no dharma." "Does a bodhisattva adorn Buddha-lands?" "No. Adorning Buddha-lands is not adorning; it is merely called adorning." "Therefore bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind like this: not giving rise to a mind abiding in form, not giving rise to a mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch or objects of mind. Without abiding anywhere, give rise to the mind. Subhūti, if a person's body were as large as Mount Sumeru, would that body be great?" "Very great. The Buddha calls what is not a body a great body."
k10.commentary: "Without abiding anywhere, give rise to the mind." It is said that the Sixth Patriarch Huineng awakened on hearing this line, the most famous in the Diamond Sutra.

k11.heading: 11. The Superior Merit of the Unconditioned
k11.plain: "Subhūti, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, would the sands of all those rivers be many?" "Very many. Those rivers alone would be countless, let alone their sands." "Now I tell you truly: if a good man or good woman filled as many great trichiliocosms as those grains of sand with the seven treasures and gave them away, would the merit be great?" "Very great." "Yet if someone receives and keeps even a single four-line verse of this sutra and explains it to others, that merit surpasses the former."
k11.commentary: The merit of passing on wisdom that abides nowhere (unconditioned merit) is greater than merit with form (conditioned merit).

k12.heading: 12. Honoring the True Teaching
k12.plain: "Moreover, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is taught, even a single four-line verse of it, know that the place should be honored by all the gods, humans and asuras of the world like a stupa of the Buddha, how much more a person who can receive, keep, read and recite it all. Subhūti, know that such a person achieves the highest, foremost and rarest Dharma. Wherever this sutra is found, there is the Buddha and his honored disciples."
k12.commentary: Honor the true teaching: where the sutra is, there the Buddha is.

k13.heading: 13. Receiving and Keeping It Rightly
k13.plain: Then Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be called, and how should we keep it?" "This sutra is called the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā; keep it by that name. The Prajñāpāramitā the Buddha speaks of is not Prajñāpāramitā; it is merely called Prajñāpāramitā. Is there a Dharma the Tathāgata has taught?" "The Tathāgata has taught nothing." "Are the motes of dust in the great trichiliocosm many?" "Very many." "The Tathāgata says the motes of dust are not motes of dust; they are merely called motes of dust. The world is not a world; it is merely called a world. Can the Tathāgata be seen by the thirty-two marks?" "No. The thirty-two marks the Tathāgata speaks of are not marks; they are merely called the thirty-two marks." "If a good man or good woman gave away lives as many as the sands of the Ganges, still the merit of one who receives and keeps even a single four-line verse of this sutra and explains it to others is greater."
k13.commentary: The sutra receives its name: wisdom that, like a diamond, cuts through every attachment. The logic "A is not A; it is merely called A" recurs again and again.

k14.heading: 14. Leaving Appearances, Perfect Stillness
k14.plain: Then Subhūti, hearing this sutra and deeply understanding its meaning, wept and said to the Buddha: "How rare, World-Honored One! Since I gained the eye of wisdom I have never heard so profound a sutra. Whoever hears this sutra with pure faith will realize true reality, and achieves the rarest merit. True reality is no-form; that is why the Tathāgata calls it true reality. For me now it is not hard to believe, understand and keep this sutra, but if five hundred years from now beings believe and keep it, they will be the rarest of people, because they will have no notion of self, person, being or life. One who has left all appearances behind is called a Buddha." "So it is, so it is. Truly rare is one who hears this sutra and is not startled, afraid or alarmed. Subhūti, the pāramitā of patience is not the pāramitā of patience. Long ago, when King Kali cut my body limb from limb, I had no notion of self, person, being or life. Had I had them, I would have felt anger and resentment. And during five hundred lives as the Sage of Patience, I had no such notions either. Therefore a bodhisattva should leave all appearances behind and set the mind on supreme awakening: not giving rise to a mind abiding in form, sound, smell, taste, touch or objects of mind, but giving rise to a mind that abides nowhere. If the mind abides somewhere, that is not true abiding. The Tathāgata speaks what is true, what is real, what is just so; he does not deceive and does not speak otherwise. A bodhisattva who gives while abiding in dharmas is like a person who enters darkness and sees nothing; one who gives without abiding in dharmas is like a person with clear eyes in sunlight who sees every color. If in the future anyone receives, keeps, reads and recites this sutra, the Tathāgata, with a Buddha's wisdom, fully knows and fully sees that they achieve measureless, boundless merit."
k14.commentary: Leaving appearances behind, all suffering is stilled. The story of King Kali, from the Buddha's past lives, shows that true patience is possible only when there is no notion of "self."

k15.heading: 15. The Merit of Keeping the Sutra
k15.plain: "Subhūti, suppose a good man or good woman gave away bodies as many as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, again at midday, and again in the evening, and did so for measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. If someone hears this sutra with faith and does not turn against it, their merit is greater, how much more if they copy it, receive and keep it, read and recite it, and explain it to others. In short, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The Tathāgata teaches it for those who have set out on the Great Vehicle, for those who have set out on the supreme vehicle. Those who keep this sutra and spread it widely carry the Tathāgata's supreme awakening on their shoulders. Those who delight in lesser teachings cling to views of self, person, being and life, and cannot hear and keep this sutra. Wherever this sutra is, that place is a stupa: all should honor it, bow, circle it, and scatter flowers and incense there."
k15.commentary: The merit of keeping the sutra. This passage also grounds the practice of copying sutras.

k16.heading: 16. Able to Purify Karmic Obstacles
k16.plain: "Moreover, Subhūti, if those who keep, read and recite this sutra are scorned by others, it is because the wrongs of their past lives would have sent them to evil realms; being scorned in this life, those past wrongs are wiped away, and they will attain supreme awakening. For countless kalpas before I met Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I met eight hundred and forty trillion nayutas of Buddhas and served and made offerings to every one of them. Yet compared with the merit of one who keeps, reads and recites this sutra in the latter age, my merit does not reach one hundredth, not one trillionth. If I described that merit in full, those who heard might be thrown into confusion, doubt and disbelief. The meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its fruit is inconceivable too."
k16.commentary: The power to purify karmic obstacles. It lets one accept even unfair treatment as old karma melting away.

k17.heading: 17. Ultimately No Self
k17.plain: Then Subhūti asked again: "How should those who set their minds on supreme awakening abide, and how should they subdue their minds?" "Give rise to the thought, 'I will liberate all beings,' yet after liberating all beings, not a single being has truly been liberated. A bodhisattva with the notion of self, person, being or life is not a bodhisattva. In truth there is not even a dharma called setting the mind on supreme awakening. Had I attained some dharma with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he would not have predicted, 'In a future age you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.' Because I truly attained no dharma, he made that prediction. Tathāgata means that all dharmas are just as they are. In the awakening the Tathāgata attained there is neither truth nor falsehood, and so it is said that all dharmas are the Buddha-Dharma. Yet all dharmas are not all dharmas; they are merely called all dharmas. A bodhisattva who says 'I will liberate measureless beings' or 'I will adorn Buddha-lands' cannot be called a bodhisattva. The Tathāgata calls a bodhisattva who has penetrated the Dharma of no-self a true bodhisattva."
k17.commentary: The question of chapter 2 returns, opening the second half of the sutra. It ends in "ultimately no self": even the notion of "I" must be emptied without remainder.

k18.heading: 18. Seeing All as One Body
k18.plain: "Subhūti, does the Tathāgata have the physical eye?" "He does." The same was asked and answered of the heavenly eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye and the Buddha eye. "If there were as many Ganges Rivers as grains of sand in the Ganges, and as many Buddha-worlds as all those grains, would they be many?" "Very many." "The Tathāgata knows all the many kinds of minds of the beings in all those worlds. Why? All the minds the Tathāgata speaks of are not minds; they are merely called minds. Subhūti, the past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped."
k18.commentary: The Buddha, possessing all five eyes, sees all as one. "The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped" is often quoted in the Seon (Zen) tradition.

k19.heading: 19. Transforming the Whole Dharma Realm
k19.plain: "Subhūti, if someone filled the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would the merit from that cause be great?" "Yes, very great." "If merit had substance, the Tathāgata would not say the merit is great. Because merit has no substance, the Tathāgata says the merit is great."
k19.commentary: Only merit made while knowing it has no substance reaches throughout the Dharma realm.

k20.heading: 20. Beyond Form and Marks
k20.plain: "Subhūti, can the Buddha be seen by a perfect body?" "No. A perfect body is not a perfect body; it is merely called a perfect body." "Can the Tathāgata be seen by his complete marks?" "No. Complete marks are not complete; they are merely called complete marks."
k20.commentary: This reconfirms the teaching of chapter 5: see the Tathāgata beyond form and marks.

k21.heading: 21. Teaching Without Anything Taught
k21.plain: "Subhūti, do not think the Tathāgata thinks, 'I have a Dharma to teach.' Whoever says the Tathāgata has a Dharma he teaches slanders the Buddha, because they have not understood my words. Teaching the Dharma means there is no Dharma to teach; that is called teaching the Dharma." Then Subhūti, the wise one, asked: "Will beings of the future hear this Dharma and have faith?" "Subhūti, they are neither beings nor non-beings. The Tathāgata says beings are not beings; they are merely called beings."
k21.commentary: He teaches, yet there is no Dharma taught. This is in the same spirit as the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra's saying that the Buddha taught all his life yet "did not speak a single word," and the two are often quoted together in Seon.

k22.heading: 22. No Dharma to Attain
k22.plain: Subhūti asked: "When the Buddha attained supreme awakening, did he attain nothing?" "So it is, so it is. In supreme awakening I attained not even the slightest dharma. That is called supreme awakening."
k22.commentary: One of the shortest chapters. Awakening is not gaining something new, but knowing what has always been so.

k23.heading: 23. Doing Good with a Pure Mind
k23.plain: "Moreover, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, with no high or low; this is called supreme awakening. Cultivating all good dharmas with a mind free of self, person, being and life, one attains supreme awakening. What are called good dharmas, the Tathāgata says, are not good dharmas; they are merely called good dharmas."
k23.commentary: Knowing emptiness does not mean giving up good deeds. Doing good with a pure mind free of clinging is itself the path to awakening.

k24.heading: 24. Merit and Wisdom Beyond Compare
k24.plain: "Subhūti, if someone heaped up the seven treasures as high as all the Mount Sumerus in the great trichiliocosm and gave them away, compared with the merit of keeping, reading and reciting even a single four-line verse of this Prajñāpāramitā Sutra and explaining it to others, it would not reach one hundredth, not one hundred-trillionth, nor could any number or comparison reach it."
k24.commentary: Merit and wisdom cannot be compared. Material merit runs out, but the merit of wisdom never does.

k25.heading: 25. Transforming Without Anyone Transformed
k25.plain: "Subhūti, do not think the Tathāgata thinks, 'I will liberate beings.' In truth there are no beings for the Tathāgata to liberate. If there were, the Tathāgata would have the notion of self, person, being and life. When the Tathāgata says 'I,' it does not mean there is a self, but ordinary people think there is. As for ordinary people, the Tathāgata says they are not ordinary people; they are merely called ordinary people."
k25.commentary: Teaching without the thought of teaching. Even the line between ordinary people and sages is not fixed.

k26.heading: 26. The Dharma Body Is Not Form
k26.plain: "Subhūti, can the Tathāgata be seen by the thirty-two marks?" "Yes, the Tathāgata is seen by the thirty-two marks." "If the Tathāgata were seen by the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning king would be a Tathāgata." "As I understand the Buddha's meaning, the Tathāgata should not be seen by the thirty-two marks." Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse: "Whoever sees me by form or seeks me by sound walks a wrong path and cannot see the Tathāgata."
k26.commentary: "Whoever sees me by form or seeks me by sound walks a wrong path and cannot see the Tathāgata" is the Diamond Sutra's second four-line verse. The Dharma body is not form.

k27.heading: 27. Neither Cut Off nor Extinguished
k27.plain: "Subhūti, do not think, 'Because the Tathāgata did not possess the marks, he attained supreme awakening.' Nor think, 'Those who set their minds on supreme awakening say that all dharmas are cut off and extinguished.' Those who set their minds on supreme awakening do not hold the view that dharmas are cut off and extinguished."
k27.commentary: A warning not to mistake "do not cling to forms" for the nihilism of "nothing exists." Emptiness is not annihilation.

k28.heading: 28. Not Receiving, Not Coveting
k28.plain: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva filled as many worlds as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and gave them away, the merit of a bodhisattva who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains acceptance is greater. Because bodhisattvas do not receive merit." "World-Honored One, why do bodhisattvas not receive merit?" "Because bodhisattvas should not cling to the merit they make, it is said that they do not receive merit."
k28.commentary: Here "acceptance" does not mean endurance, but the unshakable acceptance of the truth of no-self: acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

k29.heading: 29. Dignified and Still
k29.plain: "Subhūti, if anyone says the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, they do not understand my meaning. The Tathāgata does not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere; that is why he is called Tathāgata."
k29.commentary: This explains the meaning of the name Tathāgata. Every movement arises within a stillness that neither comes nor goes.

k30.heading: 30. The Appearance of Oneness
k30.plain: "Subhūti, if the great trichiliocosm were ground into dust, would the motes be many?" "Very many. If the motes had substance, the Buddha would not call them motes. The motes are not motes; they are merely called motes. The great trichiliocosm too is not a world; it is merely called a world. If a world had substance, it would be a single composite whole; but the single composite whole the Tathāgata speaks of is not a composite whole; it is merely called a composite whole." "Subhūti, the composite whole cannot be spoken of; only ordinary people cling to it."
k30.commentary: Whether the world is broken into dust or gathered into a whole, there is no substance. Neither parts nor whole have a fixed reality.

k31.heading: 31. Views Do Not Arise
k31.plain: "Subhūti, if someone says, 'The Buddha spoke of views of self, person, being and life,' do they understand my meaning?" "No. The views the World-Honored One spoke of are not those views; they are merely called those views." "Subhūti, those who set their minds on supreme awakening should know all dharmas like this, see them like this, believe and understand them like this, without giving rise to the notion of dharma. The notion of dharma, the Tathāgata says, is not the notion of dharma; it is merely called the notion of dharma."
k31.commentary: Do not cling even to the words that deny the view of "self." This is the stage where conceptual views no longer arise.

k32.heading: 32. Manifestations Are Not Real
k32.plain: "Subhūti, if someone filled measureless asaṃkhyeyas of worlds with the seven treasures and gave them away, the merit of a good man or good woman who has set out on the bodhisattva path and keeps, reads and recites even a single four-line verse of this sutra and teaches it to others is greater. How should they teach it to others? Without grasping at appearances, unmoving, just as it is. Why? All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and like lightning. You should see them like this." When the Buddha finished teaching this sutra, the elder Subhūti, the monks and nuns, the laymen and laywomen, and all the gods, humans and asuras of the world heard the Buddha's words, rejoiced greatly, believed, accepted and put them into practice.
k32.commentary: "All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and like lightning; you should see them like this" is the Diamond Sutra's last four-line verse, also called the Verse of Six Likenesses for its six images.

subhuti.definition: One of the Buddha's ten great disciples, called "foremost in understanding emptiness." He is the questioner of the Diamond Sutra.

tathagata.definition: "One who comes from suchness": one of the ten names of the Buddha.

bodhisattva.definition: One who seeks awakening while striving to save all beings. Bodhisattva-mahāsattva means "great bodhisattva."

anuttara.definition: Supreme, right and equal awakening: the complete awakening of a Buddha.

four-signs.definition: The notions of a self, a person, a being and a life (an eternal soul): the four attachments the Diamond Sutra again and again says to cut.

nirvana.definition: Complete nirvana in which not only afflictions but the body too has passed away without remainder.

dana.definition: Dāna: generosity. There is the giving of wealth, the giving of the Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness.

four-line-verse.definition: A verse of four lines. In the Diamond Sutra, the verses "All that has form," "Whoever sees me by form" and "All conditioned things" are the best known.

asamskrta.definition: Dharma not produced by causes and conditions: truth itself, free of arising, ceasing and change.

trichiliocosm.definition: A thousand small worlds make a small chiliocosm, a thousand of those a medium one, a thousand of those a great trichiliocosm: the boundless universe taught by one Buddha.

four-fruits.definition: The four stages of the śrāvaka's awakening: stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner and arhat.

arhat.definition: A saint who has cut off all afflictions and is no longer reborn; the highest stage of the śrāvaka.

dipankara.definition: The Buddha of the past who predicted, in one of Śākyamuni's former lives, that he would become a Buddha.

prajnaparamita.definition: The perfection of wisdom. Diamond Prajñāpāramitā means "the perfection of wisdom that cuts every attachment like a diamond."

thirty-two-marks.definition: Thirty-two excellent bodily features said to belong to Buddhas and wheel-turning kings.

paramita.definition: One of the six pāramitās: the practice of bearing insult and hardship without the mind being shaken.

kalpa.definition: An uncountably long time. A kalpa is an immeasurably long span; asaṃkhyeya means "a number that cannot be counted."

five-eyes.definition: The physical eye, the heavenly eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye and the Buddha eye.
